entries.test: Whether OpenAI's GPT-4 technical report and other public disclosures as of March 2024 left out the architecture, model size and training data details.
entries.note: The GPT-4 technical report openly said it would not give architecture or dataset details.
'Effectively stealing' is a moral label, and he hedges it with 'I would argue'. Copyright rulings could bear on it but would not settle it.

entries.test: Compare OpenAI's December 2015 founding statement and California filings with how open it was about publishing and code in 2024, to see whether the mission as practised had changed.
entries.note: The core claim is that the mission changed, which makes OpenAI's statement false. The word 'honest' adds a value judgment on top.

entries.test: Whether The New Yorker's account of the May 2016 meeting reports OpenAI leaders choosing not to correct the public belief that OpenAI meant open-sourced AI ('Please try not to correct that').
entries.note: 'Knew' points to a state of mind, but the quote he cites from the reported meeting is public evidence of it.
A proverb used as a framing device.

entries.test: Whether the image generators Marcus and Southen had discussed still produced near-copies of copyrighted characters or images in early March 2024, as shown by his posted outputs and others' tests at the time.
entries.note: Hedged with 'apparent'. The post does not say which system he tested.
